title: Emergency Medical Dispatch (EMD) Protocol
description: Emergency Medical Dispatch is the structured telephone interrogation system that turns a 911 call into a coded, prioritized response. Using the Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS), the dispatcher asks scripted key questions, assigns a determinant code such as 9-E-1 for cardiac arrest, and delivers pre-arrival instructions like CPR coaching while units roll. Every determinant maps to a response configuration, so the right resources arrive with the right urgency.

title: START Triage — Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment
description: START is the mass-casualty triage sieve used across the United States to sort dozens of patients in under a minute each. The responder checks respirations, perfusion, and mental status in that order: apneic after airway opened is expectant, over 30 breaths a minute is immediate, absent radial pulse or delayed capillary refill is immediate, failure to follow commands is immediate, and everyone else walking or stable is minor or delayed. Color tags — red, yellow, green, black — make the sort visible to every incoming crew.

title: Adult CPR with AED — AHA Chain of Survival
description: High-quality adult CPR means compressions 100 to 120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, full chest recoil, minimal interruptions, and a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio for a single rescuer. The AED is applied as soon as it arrives: power on, attach pads, clear for analysis, shock if advised, and resume compressions immediately. Each link of the chain of survival — recognition, CPR, defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care — measurably raises survival odds.

title: Incident Command System (ICS)
description: The Incident Command System is the standardized management structure every US emergency response scales on, from a car fire to a hurricane. One incident commander holds overall authority, with operations, planning, logistics, and finance/administration sections beneath, plus command staff for safety, liaison, and public information. Span of control stays between three and seven subordinates, unity of command means everyone reports to exactly one supervisor, and common terminology keeps mutual-aid crews interoperable under NIMS.

title: SCBA — Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus
description: The SCBA is the firefighter's lifeline inside an IDLH atmosphere: a pressure-demand regulator fed by a 30-, 45-, or 60-minute rated cylinder, with a facepiece, PASS distress device, and heads-up pressure display. NFPA 1981 governs its performance, and every entry follows the ritual — cylinder pressure check, buddy check of straps and seals, and PASS armed before crossing the threshold. Air management rules the fireground: crews turn back with a third of their air remaining, because the way out must be breathed too.

title: Vehicle Extrication Procedure
description: Vehicle extrication is a choreographed sequence: stabilize the vehicle against movement, manage glass and sharp edges, create space by removing doors or rolling the dash, and protect the patient with a hard shield during every cut. Crews work from the least invasive option upward — try the doors before the spreaders — while a dedicated medic stays with the patient and the incident commander tracks tool progress. NFPA 1006 sets the technical-rescue competency, and modern high-strength steels and undeployed airbags demand constant hazard reassessment.

title: Hazmat Awareness and the Emergency Response Guidebook
description: Hazmat awareness level is about recognition, not entry: identify the material from placards, labels, or shipping papers, consult the Emergency Response Guidebook for the guide number and initial isolation distances, and deny entry to everyone else. The ERG's orange pages give public-safety actions by UN number, and the green pages list evacuation distances for toxic inhalation hazards day and night. Awareness personnel never touch the product — they isolate, call for the hazmat team, and keep the hot zone empty.

title: Structural Firefighting PPE — Turnout Gear
description: Structural turnout gear is a three-layer system — outer shell, moisture barrier, thermal liner — rated under NFPA 1971 to buy survivable seconds in flashover conditions. Helmet, hood, gloves, and boots close every gap, because exposed skin is the failure point; the particulate-blocking hood is now standard as cancer-risk science has advanced. Gear is inspected after every use, washed on schedule, and retired at ten years from manufacture regardless of appearance.

title: Emergency Vehicle Operations (EVOC)
description: EVOC teaches that the emergency lights request the right-of-way — they do not grant it. Drivers train in due regard: clearing every intersection lane by lane, controlling speed so the apparatus can stop within the visible distance, and understanding that a loaded fire truck needs multiples of a car's stopping distance. NFPA 1451 and 1002 frame the qualification, and most departments re-certify on a closed course where backing, serpentine, and alley-dock maneuvers are scored.

title: Wilderness Search Patterns
description: Search theory turns lost-person behavior into math: the PLS (point last seen) anchors probability regions, and hasty search hits trails and drainages first while the confinement and attraction phases run in parallel. Grid search then sweeps high-probability segments with measured spacing matched to the search object — tighter for a child, wider for an aircraft. Robert Syrotuck's lost-person statistics tell planners how far each subject category typically travels, so resources land where the math says to look.

title: Water Rescue Awareness — Reach, Throw, Row, Go
description: Water rescue awareness ranks options by rescuer risk: reach with a pole or branch, throw a rope bag, row a boat out, and go swimming only as a trained last resort with a PFD. Drowning victims can submerge a rescuer in seconds, which is why untrained entry doubles the victim count instead of halving it. Awareness-level responders secure the scene, keep eyes on the victim, and call the water team — they do not enter the water.

title: Fireground Size-Up and RECEO-VS
description: Size-up is the continuous reading of the fireground from dispatch to overhaul: construction type, occupancy, smoke behavior, and exposures decide the strategy before a line is charged. RECEO-VS orders the objectives — Rescue, Exposures, Confinement, Extinguishment, Overhaul, then Ventilation and Salvage woven through — so the most urgent work never waits behind the merely important. A 360-degree walkaround on arrival catches the rear conditions that kill firefighters who only read the front.

title: EMS Patient Assessment — SAMPLE and OPQRST
description: Every EMS patient gets the same systematic assessment so nothing hides: scene safety and mechanism of injury first, then primary survey of airway, breathing, and circulation, then the SAMPLE history and OPQRST pain workup. SAMPLE — signs/symptoms, allergies, medications, past history, last oral intake, events leading up — turns a stranger's body into a readable record. OPQRST — onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, time — turns 'it hurts' into a clinical picture the hospital can act on.

title: Firefighter Rehabilitation Operations
description: Rehab is the incident commander's answer to the fire service's deadliest enemy — cardiac strain: crews rotate through a shaded rest area for at least ten to twenty minutes after strenuous work or SCBA cylinder depletion. NFPA 1584 requires medical monitoring in rehab — vitals, hydration, active cooling — and holds anyone whose numbers don't recover for further evaluation instead of sending them back in. Rehab is not optional rest; it is a tactical assignment with an entry log, just like the fire attack.
